analysis.one_liner: Bars credit card companies from raising your rate over unrelated credit problems.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban universal default on credit cards was introduced with 4 cosponsors in March 2009, sent to the Financial Services Committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change the Truth in Lending Act to stop credit card companies from using 'universal default' — raising the interest rate on your card because of something unrelated to that account, like a late payment to a different lender or a dip in your credit score. It would let issuers raise rates only for things you actually did on that card account, and it would require them to clearly disclose that rule. The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card holders. Millions of cardholders could face rate increases triggered by events elsewhere in their financial life — a missed bill to another company, a drop in their credit score — even if they always paid that card on time. The bill would make rate hikes tied only to that account's own payment history, and require the issuer to say so plainly in its disclosures.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a creditor from using any adverse information about a consumer — including anything in a credit report or a change in the consumer's credit score — as the basis for raising the APR on a credit card account, or for removing or increasing an introductory rate, unless the reason is the consumer's own actions on that account.

Requires credit card issuers to clearly and conspicuously describe this limitation to consumers in required disclosures and statements, so cardholders know rate hikes can only follow problems on the account itself.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, which would lose the ability to raise rates on existing balances using information unrelated to the account. Issuers argue risk-based pricing spreads costs across borrowers; banning universal default would narrow one way they priced that risk, potentially shifting some costs to fees or new-account rates.

drawbacks.text: Issuers price credit partly on a borrower's overall risk profile; prohibiting the use of adverse information could lead issuers to price new accounts higher or tighten credit for borderline borrowers to compensate for the loss of a pricing tool.

The restriction applies only to existing open-end credit card accounts under the Truth in Lending Act's credit card provisions, so some forms of risk-based repricing outside credit cards would remain lawful.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit to cardholders is real: it stops one of the more jarring practices in consumer credit, where a customer who pays on time can still see their rate jump because of events elsewhere. The main cost falls on issuers, and the bill is narrow — it addresses one pricing practice rather than the broader market. On balance it would help the people who carry credit card balances at modest cost to the industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the same day in March 2009, and the committee never took it up, so it died there when that Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Representative Keith Ellison of Minnesota introduced the Universal Default Prohibition Act of 2009 in the House on March 19, 2009, joined by four cosponsors, all Democrats.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, which was the only committee action it ever received.
The bill never advanced out of committee and never received a vote in the House or Senate before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers kept the ability to use universal default pricing, since the bill died without a vote. Cardholders did not get this protection from this bill, though broader credit card legislation passed in 2009 addressed some of the same practices through a different route.

for.name: Rep. Keith Ellison
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House on March 19, 2009.

for.name: 4 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Reps. Gutierrez, Al Green of Texas, Clay, and Cleaver).

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Barney Frank (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 19, 2009 and never scheduled a markup or reported it out.

against.name: Credit card issuers and banking industry groups
against.role: Industry affected by the ban on universal default pricing
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on raising rates on existing balances as the broader credit card debate unfolded in 2009.

sides.party_line_note: There were no roll-call votes on the bill, and all five sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats (4 of 253 House Democrats signed on), so no vote-based party split exists in the record.

industries.note: The bill would strip issuers of universal default — the ability to raise the rate on a cardholder's existing balance using credit information unrelated to that account — a tool they used to reprice risk at cardholders' expense. Cardholders who pay on time would keep their rate; issuers would lose revenue from surprise rate hikes.

industries.industry: Credit bureaus and credit scoring companies
industries.note: The bill would bar credit report and credit score information from being used to raise card rates, reducing one downstream market use of score changes, though bureaus would still sell reports for every other purpose.
